title: Units, Dimensions and Vectors — Chapter Summary
intro: This chapter sets up the toolbox every later chapter relies on: the SI system of units, dimensional analysis as a sanity check on physical equations, error analysis to quantify how trustworthy a measurement is, and vectors as the language for any quantity that has direction in space.

branches.label: Dimensions
details: [M, L, T, A, K, mol, cd]

sections.heading: Physical quantities and SI units
bullets: Every measurement = numerical value + unit.
SI defines 7 base quantities: length (m), mass (kg), time (s), current (A), temperature (K), amount (mol), luminous intensity (cd).
Common derived units: newton (N) for force, joule (J) for energy, watt (W) for power, pascal (Pa) for pressure, hertz (Hz) for frequency.
Decimal prefixes scale units across many orders of magnitude (n, μ, m, k, M, G, T).

sections.heading: Dimensions and dimensional analysis
bullets: The dimensions of a quantity say how it depends on M, L, T, A.
Force [M L T⁻²]; energy [M L² T⁻²]; power [M L² T⁻³]; pressure [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].
Principle of homogeneity: every term in a valid equation has the same dimensions.
Dimensional analysis can check equations and derive formulas up to a dimensionless constant.
Limits: it cannot find numerical constants like 2π or detect missing same-dimensions terms.

sections.heading: Significant figures and errors
bullets: Sig figs: digits that carry meaningful information about a measurement.
Multiply / divide → match sig figs to least precise input; add / subtract → match decimal places.
Errors fall into three kinds: systematic, random, gross.
Relative error = Δx / x̄; percentage error = 100 × Δx / x̄.
Combining: products / quotients add relative errors; sums / differences add absolute errors; powers multiply the relative error by the exponent.

sections.heading: Scalars and vectors
bullets: Scalar: magnitude + unit (mass, energy, time).
Vector: magnitude + direction (displacement, velocity, force).
Vectors are equal iff they have the same magnitude AND the same direction; the position of the tail is irrelevant.
Unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂ point along the +x, +y, +z axes; their magnitudes are exactly 1.
Special types: zero vector, equal vectors, negative of a vector, collinear, coplanar.

sections.heading: Vector operations
bullets: Addition: triangle / parallelogram laws; or add components: \vec{a} + \vec{b} = (a_x + b_x)î + (a_y + b_y)ĵ + (a_z + b_z)k̂.
Magnitude of a sum: |\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = √(a² + b² + 2 a b cos θ).
Dot product: \vec{a} · \vec{b} = a b cos θ; in components a_x b_x + a_y b_y + a_z b_z. Zero ⇔ perpendicular.
Cross product: |\vec{a} × \vec{b}| = a b sin θ; direction perpendicular to both by the right-hand rule. Zero ⇔ parallel.
Physics applications: work W = \vec{F} · \vec{d}; torque \vec{τ} = \vec{r} × \vec{F}.

branches.label: Cross (×)
details: Vector, magnitude = a b sin θ

key_takeaways: Units anchor every measurement; SI defines 7 base units that every other unit derives from.
Every physical equation must pass the dimensional homogeneity check; this is the cheapest sanity test in physics.
Significant figures and error propagation tell you how trustworthy your numerical answer is.
Scalars need only magnitude; vectors need magnitude AND direction.
Resolving vectors into components turns vector arithmetic into scalar arithmetic.
Dot product gives a scalar (a b cos θ); cross product gives a vector (magnitude a b sin θ, perpendicular by the right-hand rule).

glossary.definition: One of the seven units (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd) on which all derived units rest.
A unit built as a combination of base units, often given a special name (N, J, Pa, W, ...).
Symbolic representation of a physical quantity in terms of M, L, T, A, K, mol, cd.
Every term in a physically valid equation must have the same dimensions.
A digit in a measurement that carries meaningful precision information.
A repeatable, biased deviation from the true value (e.g. miscalibrated instrument).
Unpredictable fluctuation from one measurement to the next; reduced by averaging.
The ratio Δx / x̄ of mean absolute error to mean value (dimensionless).
A quantity completely described by a magnitude and a unit (no direction).
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction in space.
A vector of magnitude exactly 1, used to specify direction.
The scalar a b cos θ formed from two vectors; zero when the vectors are perpendicular.
The vector with magnitude a b sin θ and direction perpendicular to both inputs by the right-hand rule.
Convention for the direction of a cross product: fingers curl from \vec{a} to \vec{b}, thumb points along \vec{a} × \vec{b}.
